marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q001.takeaway: Fetal long-bone shafts contain red marrow; yellow marrow gradually replaces it there after early childhood.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q001.displayText:
The marrow cavity in the shaft of a fetal long bone mainly contains red marrow.

Bone marrow is a soft, pulpy tissue found in the marrow cavity and the spaces of spongy bone. It is mainly of two types:
• Yellow marrow — made predominantly of fat cells and may contain a few islands of hemopoietic tissue. It is found in the shafts of the long bones in adults.
• Red marrow — made predominantly of hemopoietic tissue. It is found throughout the skeleton of the fetus and persists until about five years of age. After that, red marrow in the shafts of long bones is gradually replaced by yellow marrow.

By around 20–25 years of age, red marrow persists in the vertebrae, sternum, ribs, clavicles, scapulae, pelvis, cranial bones, and proximal ends of the femur and humerus.

Gelatinous marrow is degenerated bone marrow in the cranial bones in old age. There is no white marrow.

rationales.b: Yellow marrow, rich in fat cells, predominates in adult long-bone shafts; fetal skeleton contains red marrow.
rationales.c: Gelatinous marrow is degenerated marrow described in cranial bones in old age, not the fetal shaft marrow.
rationales.d: The source states that there is no white marrow; the fetal shaft contains red marrow.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q002.takeaway: Osteoprogenitor cells are mesenchymal stem cells that give rise to osteoblasts.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q002.displayText: Osteoprogenitor cells give rise to osteoblasts. They are stem cells of mesenchymal origin and microscopically resemble fibroblasts. The source also illustrates the osteoprogenitor-to-osteoblast relationship and light micrographs of the two cell types.

rationales.a: Osteocytes are mature bone cells; the osteoprogenitor lineage first differentiates into osteoblasts.
rationales.c: Chondrocytes are cartilage cells, not the bone-forming descendants of osteoprogenitor cells.
rationales.d: Chondroblasts form cartilage matrix; osteoprogenitor cells give rise to osteoblasts.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q003.takeaway: Inorganic calcium hydroxyapatite is the major bone mineral; organic matrix provides toughness and tensile resistance.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q003.displayText:
Calcium phosphate, in the form of calcium hydroxyapatite, is the major constituent of the inorganic salts in bone.

Bone matrix is predominantly made up of inorganic mineral salts, which account for about 60–70% of the dry weight of bone. These salts are deposited within the organic matrix.

• Inorganic mineral salts make bone hard and rigid and provide resistance to compressive and impact forces, as in weight-bearing and jumping. Calcium phosphate as hydroxyapatite makes up about 85% of the total salts; calcium carbonate accounts for about 10%, with magnesium, chloride, fluoride, citrate, sodium and potassium also present.
• Organic matrix makes bone tough and resilient (flexible) and provides resistance to tensile forces. It consists predominantly of type I collagen, glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans and water. Osteonectin and osteocalcin are the predominant bone glycoproteins; they bind calcium and help mineralization. Other substances include chondroitin sulfates, phospholipids and phosphoproteins.

Bone histology may use decalcification: weak acids or chelating agents such as EDTA or citrate remove inorganic mineral salts. Decalcification causes bone to lose its rigidity.

rationales.a: Inorganic mineral salts make bone hard and rigid; the organic matrix makes it tough and resilient.
rationales.b: This reverses the roles: organic matrix resists tensile forces, while mineral salts resist compressive and impact forces.
rationales.d: The source assigns about 60–70% of dry bone weight to inorganic salts; the organic matrix is not about 65%.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q004.takeaway: Osteoid is the unmineralized matrix of type I collagen and gelatinous ground substance secreted during bone formation.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q004.displayText: During bone formation, mesenchymal cells and osteoblasts secrete type I collagen and gelatinous (unmineralized) matrix. Together, these form osteoid. The collagen fibers swell within the gelatinous matrix and become indistinct. Under the influence of osteoblasts, calcium salts are deposited in the gelatinous matrix; this process is mineralization. The source image shows the microscopic appearance of osteoid in osteoid osteoma.

rationales.a: Osteoblasts secrete the material, but osteoid is the matrix they produce rather than the cells plus fibers.
rationales.b: Osteoid is unmineralized; inorganic mineral salts are deposited later during mineralization.
rationales.d: Osteoid includes type I collagen and gelatinous matrix, not only the inorganic component.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q005.takeaway: Volkmann’s canals are transverse perforating canals connecting Haversian canals.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q005.displayText:
The structure marked A is Volkmann’s canal. Haversian canals communicate with one another through transverse perforating canals called Volkmann’s canals.

The Haversian system (osteon) makes up most compact bone. Each osteon has a central canal containing small blood vessels, nerves and endosteum. Multiple lamellae of calcified matrix containing type I collagen fibers surround the canal. Successive lamellae are separated by lacunae containing osteocytes. Osteocytes communicate with one another, the central canal and the osteon periphery through dendritic processes in canaliculi.

Parallel lamellae between osteons are interstitial lamellae; those near the periosteum are circumferential lamellae. On microscopy, osteons are identified by a Haversian canal with concentric lamellae, Volkmann’s canals, osteocytes with canaliculi, interstitial lamellae and circumferential lamellae.

rationales.b: A Haversian canal is the central longitudinal canal of an osteon; Volkmann’s canals connect these canals transversely.
rationales.c: Interstitial lamellae lie between osteons and are not the transverse connecting canal.
rationales.d: Circumferential lamellae lie near the periosteum; they are not Volkmann’s canals.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q006.takeaway: Membranous bones are also called dermal bones; membranocartilaginous bones develop partly from cartilage and partly from mesenchyme.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q006.displayText:
Membranous bones (not membranocartilaginous bones) are also called dermal bones. Bones are classified by their pattern of development:
• Membranous bones ossify from highly vascular membranes of primitive mesenchyme. At ossification centers, mesenchymal stem cells differentiate into osteoprogenitor cells, which give rise to osteoblasts. Examples include skull and facial bones.
• Cartilaginous bones ossify from hyaline cartilage. Osteoprogenitor cells in the deeper perichondrium contribute to bone formation. Examples include bones of the limbs, vertebral column and thoracic cage.
• Membranocartilaginous bones ossify partly from cartilage and partly from mesenchymal condensations. Examples include the clavicle, mandible, occipital, temporal and sphenoid bones.

rationales.a: Membranous bones do ossify from primitive mesenchyme, so this statement is true.
rationales.b: Cartilaginous bones develop from preformed hyaline-cartilage models, so this statement is true.
rationales.d: The clavicle is a source-listed example of a membranocartilaginous bone, so this statement is true.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q007.takeaway: Bronchi contain hyaline cartilage, whose matrix has territorial and interterritorial zones.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q007.displayText:
The cartilage shown is hyaline cartilage, which is present in bronchi.

Hyaline cartilage consists of chondrocytes and matrix. Chondrocytes in deeper matrix are rounded and may form groups of up to eight by mitotic division of one chondroblast; these are isogenous cell aggregates (cell nests). Important matrix components include type II collagen, aggrecan (a proteoglycan) and chondronectin (a glycoprotein). The basophilic matrix immediately around chondrocytes is territorial matrix; the paler matrix farther from the cells is interterritorial matrix.

On microscopy, hyaline cartilage is identified by chondrocytes in lacunae, isogenous cell aggregates, basophilic territorial and pale interterritorial matrix, and perichondrium with an outer fibrous and inner cellular layer.

rationales.a: Terminal bronchioles lack cartilage; cartilage is present in bronchi.
rationales.b: Intervertebral discs contain fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage.
rationales.d: The epiglottis contains elastic cartilage, whereas bronchi contain hyaline cartilage.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q008.takeaway: Elastic cartilage is the yellow cartilage because its matrix contains elastin fibers.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q008.displayText:
Elastic cartilage is also known as yellow fibrocartilage. It resembles hyaline cartilage: individual or small groups of chondrocytes are surrounded by type II collagen fibrils. It differs because much of its interterritorial matrix consists of fine yellow elastic fibers containing elastin.

On microscopy, elastic cartilage has chondrocytes within lacunae, elastic fibers in the matrix, and perichondrium with an outer fibrous and inner cellular layer.

rationales.a: Hyaline cartilage is not the yellow cartilage; elastic fibers give elastic cartilage its yellow appearance.
rationales.c: Fibrocartilage is the white fibrocartilage and is rich in thick collagen bundles.
rationales.d: The source names elastic cartilage as yellow fibrocartilage; “fibroelastic” is not the answer used here.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q009.takeaway: The source image shows elastic cartilage, distinguished by elastic fibers in its matrix.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q009.displayText:
The image shows elastic cartilage. Like hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage contains individual or small groups of chondrocytes surrounded by type II collagen fibrils. Unlike hyaline cartilage, much of its interterritorial matrix consists of fine yellow elastic fibers containing elastin.

On microscopy, elastic cartilage has chondrocytes within lacunae, elastic fibers in the matrix, and perichondrium with an outer fibrous and inner cellular layer.

rationales.a: Hyaline cartilage lacks the abundant elastic fibers that distinguish the cartilage in the image.
rationales.c: Articular cartilage is a specialized hyaline cartilage and does not have the elastic-fiber-rich matrix shown.
rationales.d: Fibrocartilage has thick collagen bundles and rows of chondrocytes rather than the elastic fibers described.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q010.takeaway: Verhoeff’s stain highlights elastic fibers by staining elastin dark purple or black.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q010.displayText: Verhoeff’s stain is used to visualize elastic fibers in elastic cartilage. The fibers stain dark purple or black with Verhoeff’s stain, which binds to elastin, the main constituent of elastic fibers. The source image shows elastic fibers stained in this way.

rationales.a: Hematoxylin and eosin is a general stain and is not the specific elastin stain identified in the source.
rationales.c: GMS silver stain highlights fungal organisms and basement membranes, not the elastic fibers asked about.
rationales.d: Alcian blue stains acidic mucopolysaccharides rather than specifically visualizing elastin fibers.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q011.takeaway: Fibrocartilage contains type I and type II collagen; hyaline and elastic cartilage contain type II.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q011.displayText: Type I collagen is present in fibrocartilage. Fibrocartilage (white fibrocartilage) contains both type I and type II collagen. Hyaline and elastic cartilage contain only type II collagen.

rationales.a: Hyaline cartilage contains type II collagen, not the type I collagen characteristic of fibrocartilage.
rationales.c: Elastic cartilage contains type II collagen; its distinguishing fibers are elastic fibers.
rationales.d: Articular cartilage is a hyaline-cartilage type and contains type II rather than type I collagen.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q012.takeaway: Fibrocartilage lacks perichondrium and has thick collagen bundles with rows of chondrocytes.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q012.displayText:
The image shows fibrocartilage stained with trichrome. Fibrocartilage is not covered by perichondrium. It is intermediate between dense fibrous connective tissue (tendons and ligaments) and hyaline cartilage. It consists of bundles of thick type I and type II collagen fibers, with rows of chondrocytes between the bundles.

On microscopy, fibrocartilage is identified by chondrocytes and a matrix containing abundant collagen fibers. The epiphyseal plate and bronchi have hyaline cartilage. Color should not determine cartilage type because it depends largely on the stain; the tissue’s structure and organization should be considered.
emphasis: type I and type II collagen fibers

rationales.a: The epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage, not fibrocartilage.
rationales.b: Fibrocartilage contains bundles of thick collagen fibers, not thin fibers.
rationales.d: Bronchi contain hyaline cartilage, not fibrocartilage.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q013.takeaway: Perimysium surrounds a fascicle, a bundle of skeletal muscle fibers.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q013.displayText:
Each bundle of muscle fibers (a fascicle) is surrounded by perimysium.

Skeletal muscle is organized as follows:
• A muscle fiber (myocyte) contains myofibrils and several elongated nuclei near the periphery, just beneath the cell membrane. The membrane is the sarcolemma and the cytoplasm is the sarcoplasm. Each individual muscle fiber is surrounded by delicate connective tissue called endomysium.
• A fascicle is a group of muscle fibers. Each fascicle is surrounded by perimysium, which provides a pathway for nerves and blood vessels.
• A skeletal muscle is a group of fascicles. The entire muscle is surrounded by epimysium, which contains larger nerves, blood vessels and lymphatics.

rationales.a: Epimysium surrounds the entire skeletal muscle, not each fascicle.
rationales.c: Endomysium surrounds each individual muscle fiber, not the bundle of fibers that forms a fascicle.
rationales.d: Sarcolemma is the muscle-fiber cell membrane, not connective tissue surrounding a fascicle.

marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q014.takeaway: Cardiac muscle has central nuclei, striations, branching fibers and intercalated discs.
marrow__ANAT_CH12_Q014.displayText: The image shows a longitudinal section of cardiac muscle stained with hematoxylin and eosin. On microscopy, cardiac muscle is identified by striations similar to skeletal muscle, a single centrally placed nucleus (sometimes with a perinuclear halo), and dark transverse intercalated discs at junctions between adjoining cardiac myocytes. Cells within one fiber branch and join cells in adjacent fibers.

rationales.a: Skeletal muscle has striations but typically has multiple peripheral nuclei and does not have cardiac intercalated discs.
rationales.b: Visceral smooth muscle lacks striations and intercalated discs.
rationales.d: Vascular smooth muscle also lacks the striations, branching myocytes and intercalated discs of cardiac muscle.
